claims.claim: Memory is analyzed in three stages - encoding (the initial learning of information), storage (maintaining it over time), and retrieval (accessing it when needed) - and all three must work for successful remembering.

Retrieval is cue-dependent: retrieval processes are triggered and guided by retrieval cues available in the learner's environment, so a memory that is stored can still be inaccessible when no adequate cue is present. Supplying a cue that recovers the memory shows the trace existed and the route to it did not.
The encoding specificity principle holds that a retrieval cue is effective to the extent that it matches or overlaps the memory trace of the original experience.

Baddeley and Hitch's multicomponent working memory model comprises a central executive that oversees manipulation and processing, a phonological loop for verbal and acoustic material, and a visuospatial sketchpad for visual and spatial material; an episodic buffer was added in 2000 as a temporary store that integrates information across different sensory codes.
Working memory is not merely short-term storage: it is a multicomponent system that manipulates as well as holds information, which is what distinguishes it from a passive short-term store.

Long-term memory is not unitary. Declarative (explicit) memory - knowledge available as conscious recollection - subdivides into episodic memory for specific events and semantic memory for factual knowledge, and depends on the hippocampus and surrounding medial temporal lobe. Nondeclarative (implicit) memory is an umbrella for skills and habits (striatum), priming, emotional associations (amygdala), classical conditioning (cerebellum), and nonassociative learning, and is expressed through performance rather than conscious recollection.

Patient H.M., who suffered profound declarative memory impairment after medial temporal lobe removal, retained the ability to acquire motor skills, establishing that memory is not a single entity and that skill learning depends on systems separate from declarative memory.

Processing material for meaning at study produces better retention than processing its surface form; the practical instruction from the levels-of-processing tradition is to think about the meaning of events, form associations, and create vivid mental imagery.

Craik's own 2002 retrospective on the Craik and Lockhart (1972) levels-of-processing framework addresses common criticisms and treats as open questions whether memory can be regarded as 'pure processing', how depth should be measured, encoding-retrieval interactions, and whether 'levels' of processing are real - so the framework's theoretical core remains contested even though its practical advice holds.

Ebbinghaus's forgetting data came from 163 double tests conducted in 1879-80 in which he was his own and only subject, learning series of 13 nonsense syllables to two errorless recitations and relearning them after about one third of an hour, 1 hour, 9 hours, one day, two days, six days, or 31 days, with retention measured as savings - the proportion of the original learning work saved on relearning.

Ebbinghaus's savings values fell steeply at first and then flattened: approximately 58 percent after about twenty minutes, 44 percent after an hour, 36 percent after nine hours, 34 percent after one day, 28 percent after two days, 25 percent after six days, and 21 percent after 31 days. Ebbinghaus himself described the results as special, individual, and uncertain, and judged the 33.7 percent one-day figure to be one to two units too large.

Murre and Dros (2015) successfully replicated the forgetting curve using the same savings method with a single subject who spent about 70 hours learning 70 lists of nonsense syllables and relearning them at Ebbinghaus's retention intervals. Their curve closely resembled the original except at 31 days, where savings were markedly lower (0.041 versus Ebbinghaus's 0.211), and they concluded the curve is not smooth, showing an apparent upward jump beginning around the 24-hour point that may reflect sleep.

Because both the original study and the 2015 replication used a single subject learning deliberately meaningless material with the savings method, the shape of the forgetting curve is well replicated but its specific percentages should not be quoted as rates at which students forget meaningful classroom material.

Forgetting has several distinct causes: encoding failure, decay of the trace over time, interference from competing memories, and retrieval failure. Decay theory has been criticized because disuse of a memory does not always guarantee forgetting, and modern accounts emphasize disruption of consolidation instead.

Proactive interference occurs when older memories block the learning or retrieval of newer related material; retroactive interference occurs when newer memories block the retrieval of older related material.

A meta-analysis of incidental environmental context-dependent memory found context effects reliable across studies, but showed they are reduced by noncontextual cues used during learning (overshadowing) and at test (outshining), and by mental reinstatement of the study context at test.

A 2021 replication of the Godden and Baddeley (1975) diving experiment with 16 divers failed: the original analysis found no significant interaction between learning and recall environment (F = 1.999, p = 0.163), and a 2022 addendum that reanalyzed the data as a repeated-measures ANOVA with order as a covariate produced a significant Learn-by-Recall interaction (p = 0.017) in a pattern that still did not match the original, with the author reaffirming that the study was not a successful replication.

Dunlosky and colleagues (2013) evaluated ten study techniques against four categories of variables - learning conditions, student characteristics, materials, and criterion tasks - and assigned high utility to practice testing and distributed practice; moderate utility to elaborative interrogation, self-explanation, and interleaved practice; and low utility to summarization, highlighting or underlining, the keyword mnemonic, imagery use for text learning, and rereading.

The moderate ratings reflect limited evidence rather than demonstrated failure: elaborative interrogation and self-explanation had not been adequately evaluated in educational contexts, and systematic exploration of interleaving had only begun. Most students report relying on rereading and highlighting even though these do not consistently boost performance, and the authors' recommendation is substitution - practice testing instead of rereading.

Roediger and Karpicke (2006) had students study prose passages and then either take immediate free-recall tests without feedback or restudy the same number of times. Repeated studying improved recall on a final test given after five minutes, but on final tests two days and one week later prior testing produced substantially greater retention - even though repeated studying increased students' confidence in their ability to remember.

The distributed-practice meta-analysis by Cepeda and colleagues (2006) located 839 assessments in 317 experiments across 184 articles and found that the interstudy interval producing maximal retention increases as the retention interval increases, so the optimal gap between study sessions depends on how long the material must be retained.

Brunmair and Richter's (2019) multilevel meta-analysis of interleaved learning - 59 studies, 238 effect sizes nested in 158 samples - found a moderate overall interleaving effect (Hedges' g = 0.42), largest for paintings (g = 0.67) and other visual materials, small for mathematical tasks (g = 0.34), ambiguous and non-significant for expository texts and tastes, and reversed in favour of blocking for word materials (g = -0.39). Interleaving effects were stronger for material more similar between categories, less similar within categories, and more complex.

In a survey of 242 teachers interested in the neuroscience of learning (137 in the UK, 105 in the Netherlands), 48 percent of UK teachers and 46 percent of Dutch teachers agreed with the statement that we use only 10 percent of our brain.

The claim that humans use only 10 percent of the brain is false. The brain is about 2 percent of body weight but consumes roughly 20 percent of calories, that consumption holds across activities and during sleep when the whole brain remains intensely active, and the brain's capacity to rewire after the loss of an entire hemisphere in early childhood reflects plasticity rather than spare unused capacity. The idea traces at least to William James's 1907 suggestion that people use only a small part of their possible mental and physical resources.

Memory is reconstructive rather than reproductive: learning and memory systems give people the ability to produce knowledge without storing copies of it, and memories are reconstructed anew at each recall in a way that takes account of current knowledge, expectations, and context.

The misinformation effect is the impairment of memory for a past event caused by exposure to misleading post-event information. Warnings inhibit its damaging effects only under limited circumstances, some groups are more susceptible than others, and later work in the same programme showed that people can come to believe falsely that they experienced rich, complex events that never occurred.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How much the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve licenses claims about classroom forgetting.
positions: The curve is a robust empirical regularity: Murre and Dros reproduced it closely at almost every interval using Ebbinghaus's own savings method, more than a century later and in a different language.

The curve was established by one man relearning meaningless syllables he had memorized himself, the 2015 replication also used a single subject, and the savings measure behaves unusually with easily learned material, so the quantitative values describe a narrow task rather than the forgetting of meaningful, understood classroom material.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports the replication as genuine support for the shape of the curve while stating plainly that the specific percentages come from single-subject nonsense-syllable studies and must not be quoted as rates at which students forget lessons. Ebbinghaus's own caution about his numbers, and the replication's finding that the curve is not perfectly smooth, are included rather than smoothed over.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether physical context at encoding reliably determines retrieval success.
positions: Smith and Vela's meta-analysis found environmental context effects reliable across the incidental-context literature.

The same meta-analysis found the effects shrink under overshadowing, outshining, and mental reinstatement, and a 2021 replication of the best-known demonstration - the Godden and Baddeley diving study - failed, with the 2022 addendum's reanalysis producing a significant interaction in a pattern that still did not match the original.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches encoding specificity as well supported at the level of cue-to-content overlap, and separately marks the strong version - that students must be tested where they studied - as weakly supported. The failed replication and its addendum are named rather than omitted, and the practical advice is to match the cues that carry meaning (format, prompt wording, question type) rather than the room.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether decay is a genuine cause of forgetting or whether interference and retrieval failure account for it.
positions: Trace decay was the original explanation of the forgetting curve and is still listed among the causes of forgetting.

Critics note that disuse does not guarantee forgetting, and modern accounts locate the problem in disrupted consolidation and in competition from other memories rather than in the passage of time itself.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents decay, interference, and retrieval failure as partly competing and partly complementary explanations rather than asserting one, and gives the teacher-usable diagnostic: if a cue restores the memory, the trace was not gone.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How strongly interleaving should be recommended.
positions: Dunlosky and colleagues assigned interleaving a moderate utility rating in 2013 because systematic study had only begun.
Brunmair and Richter's later meta-analysis found a moderate average effect that varies sharply by material, with blocking outperforming interleaving for word learning (g = -0.39).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson recommends interleaving for practice on categories and problem types learners confuse, and explicitly advises against interleaving word-list learning, citing the negative effect size for word materials.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What 'memory is reconstructive' entitles a teacher to say.
positions: Reconstruction plus the misinformation literature shows recollection can be distorted by information encountered after the event, and that people can acquire confident memories of events that never happened.
None of that establishes that everyday recall is generally unreliable; the same systems support accurate performance constantly.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the precise claim - retrieval is an active process that can incorporate material from outside the original episode, so confidence is not a reliable index of accuracy - and draws the teaching corollary that a confidently recalled misconception feels like a confidently recalled fact, which argues for retrieval practice with feedback rather than retrieval practice alone.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive factual claims about memory at all. Its body text was placeholder prose ('Memory And Learning is a foundational concept in Education', 'a concept students use to organize information') that named no memory system, no researcher, no study, and no study strategy, and its vocabulary list defined the topic in terms of itself.
The draft's Eli-10 analogy ('a label on a toolbox drawer', 'reading a map legend') carried no explanatory content about memory and supplied no analogy limits.
The draft's title was mis-cased as 'Memory And Learning'.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire generated draft with researched content; nothing from the draft survives except the topic coordinates.
Corrected the title case to 'Memory and Learning'.

Kept cognitive load theory, the Atkinson-Shiffrin modal model, the Miller/Cowan capacity debate, and the learning-styles debunk out of scope because education:learning-theories:cognitivism already teaches them; this lesson references that lesson rather than repeating it.

Did not carry forward two claims from the quarantined draft research that independent checking could not confirm: that the 10 percent myth originates in Karl Lashley's 'silent cortex' work and in the glia-to-neuron ratio, and that electrical stimulation during neurosurgery reveals no inactive areas. The verified MIT McGovern refutation (energy budget, whole-brain activity in sleep, plasticity, William James origin) is used instead.
